facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: It lived during the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: The first fossils of Stratiotosuchus were found in the 1980s, and the type species was named in 2001.
facts.quote: The first fossils were found in the 1980s, and the type species Stratiotosuchus maxhechti was named in 2001.

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus was a hyperpredator that likely filled ecological niches occupied by theropod dinosaurs in other regions.
facts.quote: A hyperpredator, it and other baurusuchids may have filled niches occupied elsewhere by theropod dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus had a robust, laterally compressed skull measuring 47 cm long, making it one of the largest known baurusuchids.
facts.quote: Stratiotosuchus has a robust, laterally compressed skull that is 47 cm long, among the largest known baurusuchids.

facts.statement: The teeth of Stratiotosuchus were ziphodont, meaning they were laterally compressed, curved, and serrated.
facts.quote: The teeth are ziphodont, meaning that they are laterally compressed, curved, and serrated.

facts.statement: Unlike most baurusuchids which typically have four premaxillary teeth, the holotype of Stratiotosuchus possessed only three premaxillary teeth.
facts.quote: Most baurusuchids have a reduced number of teeth, with four in their premaxilla and five in their maxilla, but Stratiotosuchus possessed only 3 premaxillary teeth on its holotype.

facts.statement: Specimens of Stratiotosuchus come from the Adamantina Formation, which dates to either the Turonian-Santonian (about 85 million years ago) or the Campanian-Maastrichtian (about 70 million years ago).
facts.quote: This skeleton and all other specimens of Stratiotosuchus come from the Adamantina Formation, which is either Turonian-Santonian in age (about 85 million years old) or Campanian-Maastrichtian in age (about 70 million years old).

facts.statement: Preparation of the holotype skeleton revealed evidence of two individuals preserved together in the same sandstone block.
facts.quote: Further preparation of DGM 1477-R revealed that two individuals were present in the same block of sandstone, as indicated by two extra leg bones, an extra fragment of the hip, and extra metatarsals.

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus has been classified as a baurusuchid since its first description in 1988.
facts.quote: Stratiotosuchus has been recognized as a baurusuchid since it was first described in 1988.

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus belongs to the clade Metasuchia, which includes living crocodilians and extinct relatives extending back into the Jurassic.
facts.quote: Stratiotosuchus and Baurusuchus both belong to a large clade called Metasuchia, which includes living crocodilians and many extinct relatives extending back into the Jurassic.

facts.statement: The exact phylogenetic position of Stratiotosuchus within the clade Metasuchia remains uncertain.
facts.quote: However, the exact position of Stratiotosuchus and Baurusuchus within Metasuchia is still uncertain.

facts.statement: According to Montefeltro et al. (2011), Stratiotosuchus belongs to the subfamily Baurusuchinae within the family Baurusuchidae.
facts.quote: Montefeltro et al. (2011) found support for baurusuchids as advanced notosuchians, and divided the family into two subfamilies, Baurusuchinae and Pissarrachampsinae. Stratiotosuchus belonged to Baurusuchinae along with Baurusuchus.

facts.statement: Riff and Kellner (2011) placed Stratiotosuchus deep within Notosuchia as the sister taxon to the family Sphagesauridae.
facts.quote: Another phylogenetic analysis of baurusuchids was conducted by Riff and Kellner (2011). Their analysis placed Stratiotosuchus and Baurusuchus deep within Notosuchia, as the sister taxon of the family Sphagesauridae.

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus had large crests over its hip socket that stabilized the hip in a pillar-erect stance.
facts.quote: Large crests are present over the acetabulum, or hip socket, stabilizing the hip in what is known as a pillar-erect stance (the acetabular crest lies like a shelf on top of the femur to form a pillar).

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus likely had a much stronger puboischiotibialis muscle than modern crocodilians, allowing it to maintain a permanent upright stance.
facts.quote: The puboischiotibialis is very weak in living crocodilians, so they cannot sustain a high walk for very long. Stratiotosuchus is thought to have had a much stronger puboischiotibialis, allowing it to have a permanent upright stance.

facts.statement: The arm socket of Stratiotosuchus faced backwards and downwards, suggesting its arms were held beneath the body.
facts.quote: The arm socket faces backwards and downwards from a bone in the shoulder girdle called the coracoid, suggesting that the arms were held beneath the body.

facts.statement: Tightly clustered metacarpals forming narrow hands and a backward-projecting calcaneal tuberosity suggest an erect posture in Stratiotosuchus.
facts.quote: Other features that suggest an erect posture are tightly clustered metacarpals forming narrow hands well-suited for walking and a backward-projecting calcaneal tuberosity in the ankle, which would have attached to muscles that fixed the lower limb in a parasagittal axis.

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus stood with a fully erect posture similar to that of bipedal theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: With a fully erect stance, Stratiotosuchus has many features convergent with theropod dinosaurs, which are fully bipedal.

facts.statement: The upper part of the femur in Stratiotosuchus has a rough surface region analogous to the accessory trochanter found in tetanuran theropods.
facts.quote: In Stratiotosuchus, a roughly surfaced region on the upper part of the femur is analogous to the accessory trochanter common to tetanuran theropods.

facts.statement: The articular surface where the tibia attaches to the femur in Stratiotosuchus is laterally compressed, unlike the circular surface in living crocodilians but similar to theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The articular surface of the tibia that attaches to the femur is laterally compressed, which is unlike the more circular surface in living crocodilians and more like that of a theropod dinosaur.

facts.statement: The parent group of Stratiotosuchus is Baurusuchinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Baurusuchinae

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus belongs to the family Baurusuchidae.
facts.quote: Family: Baurusuchidae

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Stratiotosuchus was described by Campos and colleagues in 2001.
facts.quote: Campos et al. 2001
